According to the appellant, at the time of the accident he was aged 54 years and was working as a fitter in a workshop in Nadakavu cross road, earning Rs.15,000/- per month.
The appellant therefore claimed compensation of Rs.1,16,000/-.
By the impugned award, the Tribunal granted total compensation of Rs.27,064/- with interest at the rate of 7% p.a.
Aggrieved, this appeal is filed.

sentences.text: Learned Counsel for the appellant contended that the Tribunal grossly erred in taking the notional income of the appellant as Rs.3,500/- per month.

It is contended that, even if no documents were produced to prove monthly income, the Tribunal ought to have fixed the notional income by taking guidance from the Apex Court decision in Ramachandrappa v. Manager, Royal Sundaram Alliance Insurance Co. Ltd. [(2011) 13 SCC 236].

entities.text: Ramachandrappa v. Manager, Royal Sundaram Alliance Insurance Co. Ltd. [(2011) 13 SCC 236]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Tribunal also committed illegality by denying compensation for the loss sustained by the appellant due to his permanent disability, in spite of him being certified to be suffering from 20% disability.

4. Learned Counsel for the insurance company contended that Ext.A4 disability certificate is issued by a Doctor who had not treated the appellant and the certificate was not proved by examining the Doctor.
Hence, the Tribunal was justified in refusing to accept and act upon that document.
According to the Counsel, just and proper compensation has been granted by the Tribunal.

Therefore, the impugned award warrants no 2025:KER:32983 interference.
5.
As far as the challenge against fixation of notional income is concerned, it is to be noted that the appellant had not produced any document to prove that his monthly income was Rs.4,500/-.

In such circumstances, the option available to the Tribunal was to assess the notional income, by taking guidance from the decision of the Apex Court in Ramachandrappa (supra), and in which event, the notional income would be Rs.8,000/- per month.
Be that as it may, since the appellant had claimed only Rs.4500/- as income, the said amount could have been fixed as his notional income.

6. There is also merit in the challenge against reduction of the percentage of disability, since Ext.A4 certificate was issued by the doctor after examining the appellant and perusing his treatment records.

In Dileep Antony v. Shobin Sebastian and Others [2022 (6) KHC 105], a learned Single Judge of this Court referred to G.O(P) No.161/97/H&FWD dated 15.05.1997 containing the revised orders/guidelines for issuing 2025:KER:32983 disability certificates for production before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, Workmen's Compensation Courts etc., to hold that the guidelines are to be followed by the Tribunals.

entities.text: Dileep Antony v. Shobin Sebastian and Others [2022 (6) KHC 105]

sentences.text: As per the G.O(P) No.161/97/H&FWD, the disability certificates are to be issued by a specialist doctor (Government or Private) with not less than 10 years standing in the speciality, who has not treated the patient in the acute stage after the accident.
This is to ensure unbiased and accurate assessment of the permanent disability.
The Government Order also mandates that appeals/second opinion in the case of such certificates should be referred to the State Disability Assessment Board.

7. Apart from the Government Order discussed above, Rule 387 of the Kerala Motor Vehicles Rule,
1989 ('the KMV Rules' for short) confers the Tribunal with the power to direct any Medical Officer in a Government Hospital or in a Medical College Hospital or any Board consisting of such officers to examine the injured and issue disability certificate indicating the degree and extent of disability.
As has often been repeated by this Court as 2025:KER:32983 well as the Supreme Court, the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals cannot sit as mute spectators while considering the claim for compensation.

On the contrary, the Tribunals are expected to take a pro-active role in the decision Pavithran vs M.Shajahan on 7 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125643449/
3 making process.

If the Tribunals have any doubt regarding authenticity or correctness of the certificate, a second opinion can be sought, as provided in the Government Order or in exercise of the power conferred under Rule 387 of the KMV Rules.

In the case at hand, the Tribunal has not given any valid reason for not accepting the finding in Ext.A4 disability certificate, except mentioning about the appellant's failure to examine the Doctor who issued the certificate.
The said finding cannot be sustained in the light of the Division Bench decision of this Court in Karunakaran @ Kannan v. Abdul Rasheed and Others [2015 (5) KHC 355].

entities.text: Karunakaran @ Kannan v. Abdul Rasheed and Others [2015 (5) KHC 355]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Paragraph 7 of that judgment being relevant is extracted hereunder:-
"7.The
second

reason stated by the Tribunal for rejecting Ext. A8 is that Dr. Jacob P.
J. was not the doctor who treated the appellant.
This is also unsustainable.

There is no binding 2025:KER:32983 principle that, in order to rely on a disability certificate,
it should have necessarily been issued by the doctor who treated the injured.
A Medical Board constituted in a medical college or in a district or general hospital is usually competent enough to assess and certify the disability of a person.
The Medical Board so constituted would be comprised of doctors from different disciplines.
None of them may have treated the person who is subjected to assessment.
Is it a bar for acting upon the disability certificates issued by such Medical Boards?
Certainly not.

Similarly, a competent doctor, who may not be the doctor who treated the injured,
can examine, assess and certify the disability of the injured giving the required details and reasons in his certificate.

Such a medical opinion in regard to disability,
temporary or permanent, has to be considered objectively by the Tribunal.
If it finds that the opinion of the doctor is acceptable, it is well within the powers of the Tribunal to act upon it and award compensation accordingly.
If such opinion of the doctor is found unacceptable, the Tribunal is free to reject it.
The doctor who has assessed and certified the disability not being the doctor who has treated the injured cannot be a sound reason for rejecting the disability certificate."

8.In this context, it will also be apposite to note the observation of the Apex Court in Union of India and Another v.
2025:KER:32983 Talwinder Singh [(2012) 5 SCC 480] that the opinion of the Medical Board, which is an expert body, must be given due weight, value and credence.
